strengths: SciEvents is a useful and relevant resource: 2,508 abstracts with 24,381 events and 56,411 arguments, covering hierarchical events, overlapping spans, and discontinuous arguments. Its detailed scientific discourse schema gives the contribution value beyond the proposed model.
Dataset construction includes expert schema refinement, annotator training, separate annotation and inspection, and iterative corrections. These are meaningful quality-control measures.

The experiments cover nine baselines, report three-run results, and examine challenging structural subsets. EXCEEDS achieves the best reported argument-classification and event-correlation scores, with larger improvements on discontinuous arguments.

The manuscript provides schema definitions, worked annotations, decoding pseudocode, core hyperparameters, full precision/recall results, computational costs, and a code/data link. These details substantially support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation comparability remains unresolved. Appendix C states that discriminative models are evaluated only on contiguous nuggets, whereas generative models use offset-free text evaluation. It is unclear whether Table 3 uses identical gold instances and occurrence-sensitive matching across models. A common evaluation protocol, explicit treatment of unsupported structures, and precise subset definitions are needed before the reported rankings can be confidently interpreted.

The grid representation has an unaddressed ambiguity relevant to dense events. Argument roles are stored on THL edges, while EAL edges identify only trigger-head/argument-head connections. If one span is Subject of one OutcomeFact event and Object of another, Algorithm 1 attaches both roles to both events, even when decoding a gold grid. The paper should quantify such collisions through gold encode-decode recovery and explain their handling; their actual prevalence in SciEvents is not established.

Annotation reliability is insufficiently quantified for a central dataset contribution. The 73.05% first-pass inspection acceptance rate measures workflow outcomes, rather than agreement on spans, roles, or hierarchical links. Independent annotation agreement or a held-out expert audit would strengthen confidence. Operational definitions and examples for reverse-order nuggets are also missing despite their inclusion in the benchmark.

Evidence for the specific architectural contribution is limited. Closely related word-grid approaches such as W2NER are not adequately positioned, and relevant structured extraction systems such as Mirror are discussed but not compared experimentally. The overall AC and EC improvements over Tagprime are 0.51 and 0.53 F1 points, without paired uncertainty analysis. Moreover, removing the grid refiner improves discontinuous and reverse-order extraction in Table 4, limiting claims about its benefit for complex structures.

The broader characterization of scientific text exceeds the evidence. Density comparisons across different annotation ontologies cannot isolate intrinsic properties of the underlying domains. Table 2 also leaves sub-events unreported for GENIA despite its nested event annotations, weakening the complexity comparison. The acknowledged restriction to ACL abstracts further limits generalization. The resource remains promising, but the unresolved evaluation, representation, and annotation-reliability issues keep the Findings recommendation borderline.
